findings.why: '72Hr hydration' is a specific duration claim, so it needs a study that measured hydration over 72 hours, with that qualifier shown on the ad. It repeats in the primary text with no qualifier.
findings.fix: Remove '72Hr' unless the 72-hour study is on file; if it is, keep it with a footnote naming the study. Otherwise: 'Lightweight daily moisturizer with Vitamin E & Jojoba Oil'.

findings.why: '300% hydration boost' is a result figure with no qualifier: it doesn't say what was measured, against what baseline, over how long or on how many people. As written it reads as an efficacy number nobody can check.
findings.fix: Remove the figure, or keep it only with its study qualifier on the creative. Otherwise: 'Moisturizing formula that helps lock in moisture'.

findings.why: Selling the jojoba oil as '100% natural' is the naturalness framing Minimalist explicitly rejects, and '100%' is a vague purity claim (LNG-05) rather than a stated grade or source.
findings.fix: Enriched with Vitamin E and Jojoba Oil

rule_hit_review.why: '100% natural' describes where the jojoba oil comes from; it doesn't promise a guaranteed or permanent result. The real issue is natural/purity framing, raised as LNG-03.
No safety claim is made here (no 'chemical-free', 'no side effects' or 'natural so it's safe'); '100% natural' is ingredient-origin framing, raised as an LNG-03 advisory.
'delivers instant hydration' promises an immediate result; it needs a study measuring hydration right after application, with the qualifier on the ad.
'Dermatologically Approved' is an endorsement claim, and 'approved' implies a formal approval that doesn't exist for cosmetics; it needs a specific dermatologist study on file or narrower wording.
Same 'dermatologically approved' claim in the body copy; it needs the same substantiation or narrower wording.
'2X more moisturizers' compares against an unstated baseline (an older formula or other creams); it must say what it is compared with and be substantiated.
'natural glow' describes the skin's own healthy-looking glow, not a natural-ingredient claim; the natural framing problem is '100% natural Jojoba Oil'.

tone_read: This reads as keyword-stuffed marketplace copy: long run-on feature headers, repeated mood words (deep nourishment, fresh glowing, refreshing) and big unqualified numbers (72Hr, 2X, 300%). It is calm and has no fear hooks, but it isn't Minimalist's educational voice because it never explains what Vitamin E or jojoba oil does or at what strength.
language_read: Vitamin E and Jojoba Oil are named without any concentration, and the copy leans on '100% natural' and 'Natural Jojoba Oil' framing the brand avoids. Most efficacy is hedged with 'helps', but '72Hr hydration', 'instant hydration' and '300% hydration boost' are stated as flat facts with no study scoping.
